Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) -- The United Nations Sunday launched a special tribunal to prosecute the assassins of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri. A statue of slain former Lebanese prime minister Rafiq Hariri stands in Beirut. The tribunal convened at The Hague more than four years after Hariri was killed in a massive car bombing in Beirut on February 14, 2005. The bomb, detonated as Hariri's armored motorcade passed through Beirut's fashionable seaside Corniche district, contained hundreds of pounds of explosives. It left buildings shattered and streets littered with the mangled wreckage of vehicles. The blast also killed 22 other people. The Lebanese army was out in force on the streets of Beirut Sunday as people turned out to pay their respects to Hariri, who is buried downtown in the Lebanese capital. The U.N. tribunal will have 11 judges, whose identities are being kept secret for their safety. Four will be Lebanese. The prosecution could take as long as 10 years, sources close to the tribunal said. Four senior Lebanese generals are being held over the bombing, which also killed 22 other people. But many Lebanese -- as well as the United States and U.N. investigators -- believe Syria ordered the assassination. Syria denies it. The tribunal's prosecutor, Daniel Bellemare, refused to commit when asked at a news conference Sunday if Syrians would be charged. He said the public would have to wait and see. The U.S. State Department pledged its continued support of Lebanese judicial authorities and the tribunal's operations. The United States has promised to contribute $14 million; a request for an additional $6 million is pending approval from Congress. In a statement issued Sunday, acting State Department spokesman Robert A. Wood said Hariri's death "was an unsuccessful attempt to undermine Lebanon's sovereignty." He added: "The Lebanese people answered his assassination with the Cedar Revolution, leading to the withdrawal of Syrian troops and the most democratic Lebanese elections in decades." At the time of Hariri's death, neighboring Syria had immense political influence in the country, and had maintained troops in its smaller neighbor since the 1980s, after the fighting between Israel and the PLO in Lebanon. Hariri was admired for spearheading the rebuilding of Beirut after the country's civil war, from 1975 to 1990, and many Lebanese blamed Syria for the killing, citing Hariri's patriotism and strong sense of Lebanese independence. The killing sparked widespread protests that led to the eventual withdrawal of Syrian troops from Lebanon and the election of an anti-Syrian bloc in parliament. The anti-Syrian movement is known as the March 14 Alliance, named after the day millions of supporters of Hariri took to the streets, and its actions have been dubbed the Cedar Revolution, for the nation's iconic cedar trees. Huge counter-protests also were staged by Lebanese supporters of Syria. Along the way, U.N. investigators tasked to probe the attack found links between Syria's government and Hariri's assassination. The Lebanese hope the tribunal will settle the case, but there are also fears it could further divide the nation and open up older wounds in the country. The special tribunal takes over from the Beirut-based International Independent Investigation Commission, which looked into 20 other attacks and found elements linking some of them to a criminal network behind the Hariri killing, the United Nations said. The trial will take place in a converted gymnasium in a suburb of The Hague. The U.N. says the case is expected to be ready for trial by 2010. --CNN's Cal Perry contributed to this report.

BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) — On Sunday, the United Nations formally established a special court in The Hague to try those responsible for the assassination of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri. A monument to the slain leader, also spelled Rafiq Hariri, stands in Beirut.

The tribunal began operating more than four years after Hariri’s death on February 14, 2005. He was killed when a vehicle packed with hundreds of pounds of explosives detonated as his armored convoy traveled through Beirut’s upscale seaside Corniche area. The explosion destroyed nearby buildings, scattered twisted vehicle debris across the streets and claimed the lives of 22 other people.

Lebanese troops maintained a heavy presence throughout Beirut on Sunday while crowds visited Hariri’s burial site in the capital’s downtown district to honor him.

For security reasons, the names of the tribunal’s 11 judges have not been disclosed. Four of the judges are Lebanese. People familiar with the court said the prosecution process could last up to a decade.

Four high-ranking Lebanese generals remain in custody in connection with the bombing. Many people in Lebanon, along with U.S. officials and U.N. investigators, suspect that Syria directed the assassination, an allegation Damascus rejects.

At a Sunday news conference, tribunal prosecutor Daniel Bellemare declined to say whether any Syrians would face charges, telling the public it would have to wait for the answer.

The U.S. State Department reaffirmed its backing for both Lebanon’s judicial authorities and the work of the tribunal. Washington has pledged $14 million, while a further $6 million request awaits congressional authorization.

In a statement released Sunday, acting State Department spokesman Robert A. Wood described Hariri’s killing as “an unsuccessful attempt to undermine Lebanon’s sovereignty.” He said the Lebanese response was the Cedar Revolution, which resulted in Syrian forces leaving the country and produced Lebanon’s most democratic elections in decades.

When Hariri was assassinated, Syria exercised enormous political power in neighboring Lebanon. Syrian forces had been stationed in the smaller country since the 1980s, following fighting there between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization.

Hariri earned widespread respect for leading efforts to reconstruct Beirut after Lebanon’s 1975–1990 civil war. Many Lebanese, pointing to his patriotism and firm commitment to Lebanese independence, held Syria responsible for his death.

The assassination triggered mass demonstrations that ultimately helped force Syrian troops to withdraw and led to the election of an anti-Syrian parliamentary coalition. That political movement became known as the March 14 Alliance, after the date on which millions of Hariri supporters filled the streets. Its campaign was called the Cedar Revolution, a reference to Lebanon’s emblematic cedar trees. Large rival demonstrations were also organized by Lebanese groups supportive of Syria.

During their inquiry, U.N. investigators reported discovering connections between the Syrian government and Hariri’s assassination.

Many Lebanese hope the tribunal will finally resolve the case. At the same time, some worry that the proceedings could deepen national divisions and revive longstanding grievances.

The court replaces the Beirut-based International Independent Investigation Commission. According to the United Nations, that commission also examined 20 other attacks and found evidence suggesting that some were connected to the same criminal network implicated in Hariri’s killing.

Proceedings will be held in a former gymnasium converted into a courtroom in a suburb of The Hague. The United Nations expects the case to be prepared for trial by 2010.

CNN’s Cal Perry contributed to this report.

The United Nations-backed Special Tribunal for Lebanon began operating near The Hague in March 2009, with 11 Lebanese and international judges tasked with prosecuting those responsible for the assassination of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri. Hariri and 22 others were killed on February 14, 2005, when a massive car bomb exploded as his motorcade traveled through central Beirut. The attack also wounded more than 200 people and intensified fears that Lebanon’s fragile political system was being manipulated through violence and foreign interference.

Hariri had become a prominent opponent of Syria’s extensive political and military influence in Lebanon. His killing therefore immediately generated suspicions of Syrian involvement, although Damascus repeatedly denied responsibility. The assassination prompted enormous demonstrations known as the Cedar Revolution, during which Lebanese protesters demanded an international investigation, the withdrawal of Syrian forces, and greater national independence. Under intense domestic and international pressure, Syria ended its nearly three-decade military presence in Lebanon in April 2005.

Following a United Nations investigation, Lebanon and the UN negotiated the creation of a special court combining elements of Lebanese and international law. The tribunal was ultimately established through UN Security Council Resolution 1757 after political divisions in Lebanon prevented the agreement from being formally ratified. Based in Leidschendam, outside The Hague, the court included trial and appeals chambers, an independent prosecutor, a registry, and a defense office. Its mandate initially focused on the Hariri bombing but allowed jurisdiction over other attacks deemed legally connected to it.

The United States strongly supported the tribunal, providing both financial assistance and diplomatic backing. Washington presented the court as an important step toward ending Lebanon’s long history of political assassinations and impunity. Other governments also contributed funding, while Lebanon was responsible for a substantial share of the tribunal’s budget.

The court’s establishment was nevertheless controversial. Supporters regarded it as a vital mechanism for accountability and a defense of Lebanese sovereignty. Opponents argued that it had become politicized and could deepen tensions among Lebanon’s competing factions. Those divisions reflected the broader regional struggle involving Syria, Iran, the United States, and their respective Lebanese allies.

Despite these disputes, the tribunal represented an unprecedented international effort to investigate and prosecute a major act of political violence in Lebanon. Its launch sought not only to identify those responsible for Hariri’s assassination but also to demonstrate that attacks intended to reshape Lebanese politics through terror would be subject to judicial scrutiny rather than ignored or settled through political compromise.

**UN-backed tribunal opens in The Hague for Hariri assassination case**

**THE HAGUE, Netherlands** — A United Nations-backed tribunal has begun work in the Netherlands to prosecute those responsible for the 2005 assassination of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri, marking a new phase in the international effort to bring his killers to justice.

Hariri and 21 others were killed on February 14, 2005, when a massive truck bomb exploded near his motorcade in central Beirut. The attack shook Lebanon, triggered widespread protests and intensified international pressure that led to the withdrawal of Syrian forces from the country.

The Special Tribunal for Lebanon, based in Leidschendam near The Hague, was established through an agreement between Lebanon and the United Nations and authorized by the U.N. Security Council. It combines Lebanese criminal law with international judicial procedures.

U.N. officials said the court would operate independently and focus on individuals allegedly responsible for the bombing and potentially connected attacks. Unlike most international tribunals, it has jurisdiction over a terrorist offense under Lebanese law and may conduct proceedings in absentia if suspects cannot be taken into custody.

Supporters have described the tribunal as an important step toward ending Lebanon’s long history of political violence and impunity. Critics, however, have warned that the court could deepen political divisions inside the country.

The investigation initially examined possible Syrian involvement, allegations Damascus repeatedly denied. Attention later shifted toward members of Hezbollah, which also rejected the accusations and called the tribunal politically motivated.

Hariri, a billionaire businessman who served multiple terms as prime minister, played a central role in Lebanon’s post-civil-war reconstruction. His death remains one of the most consequential political assassinations in the modern Middle East.

# BREAKING: Special Tribunal for Lebanon Opens to Prosecute Hariri Assassination

**THE HAGUE, March 1, 2009** — An international tribunal created to prosecute those responsible for the 2005 assassination of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri officially began work today, nearly four years after the bombing that transformed Lebanon’s political landscape.

Hariri was killed on **February 14, 2005**, when a massive explosives-laden vehicle detonated beside his motorcade near Beirut’s seafront. The blast killed Hariri and **21 other people**, injured more than 200, and devastated surrounding buildings.

Suspicion quickly focused on **Syria**, which maintained a powerful military and political presence in Lebanon at the time, as well as on its Lebanese allies. Syrian authorities repeatedly denied involvement. Early United Nations investigations reported evidence pointing toward the possible involvement of senior Syrian and Lebanese security officials, though the tribunal’s task is to establish individual criminal responsibility rather than presume the guilt of any government.

The **Special Tribunal for Lebanon**, based near The Hague, was established through an agreement between Lebanon and the United Nations and brought into force by the U.N. Security Council in 2007 after Lebanon’s political divisions prevented parliamentary ratification. It will apply Lebanese criminal law while operating with international judges, prosecutors, and procedural safeguards.

Washington strongly backed the tribunal. The **United States had contributed about $14 million by the time of its launch**, making it one of the leading donors. The court is financed through voluntary international contributions covering 51 percent of its budget, with Lebanon responsible for the remaining 49 percent.

Hariri’s assassination triggered enormous demonstrations in Beirut known as the **Cedar Revolution**. Protesters demanded an independent investigation, an end to Syrian influence, and the withdrawal of Syrian troops stationed in Lebanon since the civil-war era. Under intense domestic and international pressure, Syria withdrew its forces in April 2005, ending almost three decades of military presence.

Supporters are calling today’s opening a landmark step against political assassination and impunity. Critics, including Syria and its Lebanese allies, have accused the tribunal of being politically influenced.

No suspects were on trial as the court formally opened, and investigators cautioned that prosecutions could take years.

**Special Tribunal Opens New Front in Lebanon’s Search for Justice**  
*By Staff Correspondent*  

**BEIRUT, March 2009** — Four years after a massive truck bomb killed former Lebanese prime minister Rafik Hariri and 22 others on Beirut’s seafront, an international tribunal has begun work in the Netherlands amid high expectations, deep political suspicion and warnings that its findings could again shake Lebanon’s fragile political order.

The Special Tribunal for Lebanon, based at Leidschendam near The Hague, formally commenced operations on March 1. Created by agreement between Lebanon and the United Nations and brought into force by the Security Council after the accord stalled in Beirut, it is the first international tribunal empowered to prosecute terrorism as a distinct crime under a national legal code.

Its immediate task is to identify and try those responsible for the February 14, 2005 assassination of Hariri. Its jurisdiction could also extend to other attacks committed between October 1, 2004, and December 12, 2005, if judges find that they were connected to the Hariri bombing. Later attacks may be added with the consent of Lebanon and the Security Council.

The tribunal is not beginning with an indictment, and no suspect has yet been convicted or formally identified by its prosecutor. That distinction is important in Lebanon, where political factions have long treated competing theories about the killing as established fact.

### A mixed Lebanese and international court

The tribunal combines Lebanese and international judges and applies Lebanese criminal law, modified by its statute and rules. It cannot impose the death penalty or forced labor, punishments available under Lebanese law. It may, however, hand down prison sentences, and unlike most international criminal courts it can conduct trials in absentia under specified safeguards.

Belgian judge Daniel Fransen serves as the pre-trial judge, responsible for reviewing indictments, supervising aspects of the investigation and ruling on questions concerning suspects and evidence before any case reaches trial.

The Trial Chamber includes Swiss judge Robert Roth, who serves as presiding judge, Lebanese judge Micheline Braidy and Australian judge David Re. Lebanese judge Walid Akoum and Italian judge Nicola Lettieri were named alternate trial judges.

The Appeals Chamber is led by Italian jurist Antonio Cassese, the tribunal’s first president and a prominent figure in international criminal law. Cassese previously served as the first president of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. Lebanese judge Ralph Riachy is vice-president. The other appeals judges are Afif Chamseddine of Lebanon, Kjell Björnberg of Sweden and Janet Nosworthy of Jamaica.

The court’s composition is intended to give it both Lebanese legal grounding and international independence. Yet that hybrid structure also exposes it to criticism from opposite directions: some Lebanese fear foreign interference, while others question whether institutions connected to Lebanon’s divided political system can remain insulated from local pressure.

### Bellemare takes over the investigation

The prosecution is led by Daniel Bellemare, a veteran Canadian prosecutor and former deputy attorney general. Bellemare took over the United Nations International Independent Investigation Commission in January 2008 from Belgian prosecutor Serge Brammertz and became the tribunal’s prosecutor when the court opened.

His office inherits years of evidence gathered by successive United Nations investigators, beginning with German prosecutor Detlev Mehlis. That material includes witness statements, telecommunications analysis, forensic evidence and information concerning the Mitsubishi Canter van believed to have carried the bomb.

Bellemare has adopted a markedly restrained public style. Unlike the investigation’s early period, when reports and witness claims fueled intense speculation, he has disclosed little about potential suspects or the direction of the case. His position is that evidence should be tested in court rather than debated through leaks and political statements.

That secrecy has frustrated Lebanese eager for answers, but it may also be essential to rebuilding confidence after controversies surrounding several early witnesses. Bellemare must determine which evidence is reliable enough to support indictments under judicial scrutiny, not merely which allegations appear plausible in an investigative report.

The prosecutor faces formidable challenges. The bombing scene was chaotic, evidence may have been lost or contaminated, and years have passed since the attack. Any case may rely heavily on technical records and circumstantial evidence. The tribunal also has no police force of its own and will depend on states—particularly Lebanon—to arrest suspects, provide documents and protect witnesses.

### The four generals

One of the tribunal’s first and most sensitive issues concerns four senior Lebanese security officials detained in Lebanon since August 2005:

- Major General Jamil al-Sayyed, former head of General Security;  
- Major General Ali al-Hajj, former director-general of the Internal Security Forces;  
- Brigadier General Raymond Azar, former head of military intelligence;  
- Brigadier General Mustafa Hamdan, former commander of the Presidential Guard.

The four men occupied powerful posts during the period when Syria exercised dominant influence over Lebanese security and politics. They were detained by Lebanese authorities following recommendations made during the early phase of the United Nations investigation. They have not been formally charged with Hariri’s murder and deny involvement.

Their prolonged detention has become a major political and legal controversy. Their supporters describe them as political prisoners and argue that their confinement rests on unreliable testimony. Hariri’s allies respond that their cases must be evaluated by an independent judicial authority rather than settled through political pressure.

With the tribunal now operational, Lebanese authorities must transfer control over persons and material connected to its jurisdiction when requested. Fransen, as pre-trial judge, will have to consider Bellemare’s assessment of the available evidence and decide whether continued detention is justified. The tribunal’s rules require judicial grounds for holding suspects; past political status or public suspicion alone will not be sufficient.

The decision will be closely watched. Continued detention could be interpreted by the opposition as confirmation that the tribunal is being used against figures associated with Syria. Release, meanwhile, could be portrayed by Hariri’s opponents as proof that the original investigation was flawed—even though release for lack of sufficient evidence would not necessarily establish innocence or end the broader inquiry.

### Born out of Lebanese deadlock

Hariri’s assassination triggered enormous demonstrations, the collapse of the pro-Syrian government and the withdrawal of Syrian forces after nearly three decades in Lebanon. It also divided the country into rival political camps.

The March 14 coalition, led by Hariri’s son Saad and his allies, has presented the tribunal as a means of ending Lebanon’s history of political assassination without accountability. Hezbollah, Amal and other members of the opposition have said they support justice in principle but have voiced fears that the tribunal could be politicized or used to pressure Syria and its Lebanese allies.

The court itself emerged from that domestic struggle. Negotiations produced a draft agreement between the United Nations and Lebanon, but Lebanon’s constitutional institutions could not complete ratification amid the confrontation between the government and opposition. In May 2007, the Security Council adopted Resolution 1757 under Chapter VII of the UN Charter, bringing the tribunal statute into force internationally.

For supporters, that step rescued the project from paralysis. Critics argue that it bypassed Lebanese constitutional procedures and gave the tribunal the appearance of an externally imposed institution.

Lebanon is responsible for 49 percent of the tribunal’s budget, with the remainder funded through voluntary international contributions. That commitment may become contentious if proceedings last many years or if the country’s economy deteriorates.

### Potential consequences for Lebanon

The tribunal could have several sharply different effects.

If it produces credible indictments supported by transparent evidence and fair proceedings, it could mark a break with Lebanon’s tradition of unresolved political killings. Successful prosecutions might strengthen the principle that senior officials, intelligence officers and political actors are not immune from criminal accountability.

But an indictment touching a major Lebanese faction, Syria or another regional power could inflame sectarian and political tensions. Hariri was Lebanon’s most prominent Sunni leader, while the rival alliances are linked to broader regional competition involving Syria, Iran, Saudi Arabia, France and the United States. Legal findings will therefore be interpreted through a geopolitical lens, regardless of the tribunal’s efforts to remain independent.

Trials in absentia could create an additional problem. They would allow proceedings to continue if suspects cannot be arrested, but verdicts delivered without defendants physically present may be dismissed by opponents as symbolic or one-sided. The tribunal’s legitimacy will depend on the quality of its evidence, the rights afforded to the defense and the clarity of its judgments.

There is also the risk of renewed violence. Lebanese leaders have repeatedly warned against allowing the tribunal to become a pretext for internal confrontation. Memories remain fresh of the street fighting and political crisis that culminated in the May 2008 clashes and the subsequent Doha agreement.

For now, the tribunal’s opening offers neither a quick verdict nor a complete account of the assassination. Bellemare must first decide whether the accumulated evidence can sustain charges, Fransen must review any proposed indictments, and Lebanon and other states must cooperate with the court’s orders.

The court’s ultimate influence may therefore extend beyond the identity of Hariri’s killers. It will test whether an internationalized legal process can establish facts in a country where assassinations are routinely absorbed into competing political narratives—and whether justice can be pursued without destabilizing the state it is intended to serve.

**Hariri tribunal opens as Lebanon confronts legacy of 2005 bombing**

**THE HAGUE, March 1, 2009** — An international tribunal established to prosecute those responsible for the assassination of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri formally began work on Sunday, nearly four years after the bombing that transformed Lebanon’s political landscape.

Hariri and 22 other people were killed on Feb. 14, 2005, when a huge explosion struck his motorcade near Beirut’s waterfront. The attack prompted mass demonstrations in Lebanon and intensified international pressure on Syria, which had maintained troops and extensive political influence in the country for nearly three decades.

Early United Nations investigators reported evidence pointing toward the possible involvement of senior Syrian and Lebanese security officials. Damascus has repeatedly denied any role in the killing, and no one has yet been convicted.

The Special Tribunal for Lebanon, based near The Hague and created through an agreement between Lebanon and the United Nations, will apply Lebanese criminal law with international judges and prosecutors. Its opening marks the first time an international court has been established to try a terrorist attack against a specific individual.

Four Lebanese generals have been held in Lebanon since 2005 in connection with the investigation, although they have not been formally charged. Tribunal officials are expected to review their detention and decide whether to request their transfer or release.

Hariri’s death helped trigger the “Cedar Revolution,” a wave of demonstrations that contributed to Syria’s withdrawal of its remaining troops from Lebanon in April 2005. But the assassination also deepened Lebanon’s political divisions.

The Western- and Saudi-backed March 14 coalition, led in part by Hariri’s son Saad, has accused Syria and its Lebanese allies of obstructing the investigation. The rival March 8 camp, which includes Hezbollah and parties close to Damascus, has warned that the tribunal could be politicized.

The years since the bombing have brought further assassinations, a devastating 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah, prolonged political paralysis and armed clashes in Beirut in May 2008. A Qatari-brokered agreement later that month produced a national unity government and ended an 18-month presidential vacuum.

The tribunal begins its work as Lebanon prepares for parliamentary elections in June. Supporters say it could end a long tradition of impunity for political killings. Critics fear that indictments—particularly if they implicate Syrian officials or powerful Lebanese factions—could reopen tensions in a country still divided over its relationship with Damascus and the role of Hezbollah.

No trial date has been set, and investigators have not publicly identified any suspects. Tribunal officials say proceedings could take years.
